items.title: Pebbble
items.text: What: A handcrafted stone with a hidden NFC chip. Tap it to a phone, hear a parent's voice.

items.title: Pebbble
items.text: End-to-end encrypted, stored on IPFS, decrypted only by physical possession of the object.

items.title: Pebbble
items.text: Why: We have dematerialised the things that carry memory — the voice, the touch, the object on the nightstand.

items.title: Pebbble
items.text: Co-parenting apps track schedules. Messaging tools store everything on servers that can be subpoenaed.

items.title: Pebbble
items.text: None of them were designed for a three-year-old who cannot read, or for a family where distance is not chosen but imposed.

items.title: Pebbble
items.text: How: Client-side AES-256-GCM encryption, IPFS for censorship-resistant storage, NFC serial number as key derivation input.

items.title: Pebbble
items.text: No accounts, no server, no database of messages. The system is incapable of betraying its users — not by policy, but by architecture.

items.title: Pebbble
items.text: Proof: Working PWA with dual playback modes (persistent and ephemeral).

items.title: Pebbble
items.text: The architecture designed for the hardest case serves every other case trivially.

items.title: Pebbble
items.text: -- Role: Creator & Lead Designer/Engineer Stack: Vanilla JS, Web Crypto API (AES-256-GCM, PBKDF2), Web NFC, IPFS/Pinata, Dexie.

items.title: Pebbble
items.text: js Period: 2024–present "Loin des yeux, loin du cœur. " Far from the eyes, far from the heart.

items.title: Pebbble
items.text: — French proverb The proverb exists in every language because the pain exists in every culture.

items.title: Pebbble
items.text: Distance erodes presence. Absence, sustained long enough, becomes its own kind of loss — not the sharp grief of death, but the slow fade of connection stretched too thin.

items.title: Pebbble
items.text: We have dematerialised most of what carries memory. The letters are gone.

items.title: Pebbble
items.text: The photo albums are in a cloud. The voice that said goodnight is a notification on a screen that was already dismissed.

items.title: Pebbble
items.text: We traded physical presence for digital convenience and lost something we cannot name but feel every day.

items.title: Pebbble
items.text: Some distances are chosen. The parent who works across time zones, who trades bedtime stories for quarterly targets.

items.title: Pebbble
items.text: The sacrifice made for provision, paid in presence.

items.title: Pebbble
items.text: Some distances are imposed. The military family whose parent serves on foreign soil, whose calls come at strange hours if they come at all.

items.title: Pebbble
items.text: And some distances are stolen. The child taken across a border.

items.title: Pebbble
items.text: The parent left searching. The silence that authorities cannot even quantify.

items.title: Pebbble
items.text: Behind every uncounted case is a parent who cannot hold their child.

items.title: Pebbble
items.text: A child who cannot hear their parent's voice. I am personally familiar with this silence.

items.title: Pebbble
items.text: An entire industry looked at these families — all of them, from the business traveler to the abducted child — and offered them scheduling apps.

items.title: Pebbble
items.text: The first attempts were not stones. They were logbooks — heavily tech-oriented memory systems capturing text, pictures, timestamps, anchors in time.

items.title: Pebbble
items.text: They failed the way most technology fails families: by assuming literacy, by demanding interaction, by feeling like documentation rather than connection.

items.title: Pebbble
items.text: A three-year-old cannot read a logbook. A six-year-old does not find comfort in a timestamped archive.

items.title: Pebbble
items.text: These systems recorded presence. They did not deliver it.

items.title: Pebbble
items.text: Language, persistence, reading ability — each became a constraint that narrowed the question: which stimulus triggers not the recall of a memory, but the feeling of a reconforting presence?

items.title: Pebbble
items.text: The research pointed in one direction. The human brain treats a familiar voice as a neurobiological safety cue.

items.title: Pebbble
items.text: A child recognizes their parent's voice from birth. By two months, that voice is encoded as a marker of safety — a familiar voice evokes the entire mental representation of a person, including visual memories and emotional context, even in the absence of a face.

items.title: Pebbble
items.text: Neuroscience has a clinical term for what a parent's voice does to a child's nervous system: non-pharmacological anxiolytic.

items.title: Pebbble
items.text: It reduces anxiety without medication. Not image, not video, not text.

items.title: Pebbble
items.text: Voice carries the message, the sentiment, the emotions, and most importantly — the presence.

items.title: Pebbble
items.text: The physiology is unambiguous. Hearing a loved one's voice triggers a measurable cortisol reduction — stress suppression — and a significant increase in oxytocin, the hormone that mediates bonding.

items.title: Pebbble
items.text: Text messaging produces neither. No cortisol change. No oxytocin release.

items.title: Pebbble
items.text: Physiologically identical to the control group. A text says "I love you.

items.title: Pebbble
items.text: " A voice makes the body believe it.

items.title: Pebbble
items.text: A study of 1,772 participants found that voice-only communication consistently outperforms video in empathetic accuracy — the ability to correctly identify what another person is feeling.

items.title: Pebbble
items.text: Removing visual input forces the brain to focus entirely on paralinguistic cues: tone, inflection, rhythm.

items.title: Pebbble
items.text: Video calls can paradoxically increase distress in children by highlighting physical absence.

items.title: Pebbble
items.text: The screen shows the parent's face but confirms they are not here.

items.title: Pebbble
items.text: Voice does not carry that contradiction. Voice accompanies. It does not remind you of what is missing.

items.title: Pebbble
items.text: Emotional voices are not only recognised more accurately — they are retained better over time.

items.title: Pebbble
items.text: After one week, the memory trace of an emotional voice is nearly twice as strong as a neutral one.

items.title: Pebbble
items.text: A parent's voice saying goodnight is not just heard in the moment.

items.title: Pebbble
items.text: It persists. The brain holds onto it because it matters.

items.title: Pebbble
items.text: A voice in the dark is a presence. A text in the dark is information.

items.title: Pebbble
items.text: Technology announces itself. Screens glow. Devices demand charging.

items.title: Pebbble
items.text: Gadgets require learning, updating, maintaining. A stone does not announce itself.

items.title: Pebbble
items.text: A stone on a nightstand is invisible. A stone in a pocket is unremarkable.

items.title: Pebbble
items.text: A stone in the hands of a child being monitored raises no suspicion.

items.title: Pebbble
items.text: The object needed to be convenient — something that fits in a child's pocket, something you could always have with you.

items.title: Pebbble
items.text: Watching children explore their surroundings, one thing always appealed to me: a cross-gender constant, older than any toy.

items.title: Pebbble
items.text: Children collect stones. Simple, dirty stones, cherished like the most precious discovery of the day — sometimes of a life.

items.title: Pebbble
items.text: No child has ever been taught to pick up a stone. They just do.

items.title: Pebbble
items.text: Each Pebbble is hand-shaped from a water-based composite that solidifies on contact with air and reproduces the exact texture and feel of a river pebble — same grain, same weight, same way it warms progressively in your hand as you hold it.

items.title: Pebbble
items.text: The material allows shaping around water-resistant, sealed NFC tags without seams, without molding marks, without any visible sign that it holds anything at all.

items.title: Pebbble
items.text: People discovering it for the first time try to see how it opens, what it contains.

items.title: Pebbble
items.text: There is nothing to find. It is a stone.

items.title: Pebbble
items.text: A child might find it interesting at first. But the relationship with the stone changes when they realise it is coated with a fine luminescent layer that makes it glow in the dark — distinguishing it from every other pebble in their collection.

items.title: Pebbble
items.text: And it changes again, permanently, when they witness it connect to a phone and hear a voice they love.

items.title: Pebbble
items.text: Not just another nice pebble. A magical one. Like the pebbles from Le Petit Poucet — the stones that lead him and his brothers and sisters back through the forest, back to their family, back to their loved ones.

items.title: Pebbble
items.text: That is where the stone comes from.

items.title: Pebbble
items.text: Inside each one: an NFC chip. No battery. No screen. No moving parts.

items.title: Pebbble
items.text: Twelve cents of hardware that draws power only at the moment of reading, then waits again.

items.title: Pebbble
items.text: It will wait for decades. Hold the stone to a phone. Hear your parent's voice.

items.title: Pebbble
items.text: A child does not need to understand IPFS or NFC. They need to understand: hold this to the phone, and you hear mama's voice.

items.title: Pebbble
items.text: I collected reference pebbles from a river. They stand aligned in a box on my desk — guides for shape and weight.

items.title: Pebbble
items.text: Hand-shaping these stones has something relaxing about it, leaning towards meditation.

items.title: Pebbble
items.text: The constraint was finding a material clean enough — non-toxic once cured, safe for a child who will carry it everywhere.

items.title: Pebbble
items.text: Once solved, the process became straightforward. The complexity lives elsewhere.

items.title: Pebbble
items.text: What lasts is simple. What matters should last. Design for the extreme case and the common case becomes trivial.

items.title: Pebbble
items.text: The extreme case: no reliable internet, active censorship, a monitored device, a child too young for interfaces, content that must survive hostile infrastructure, technology that must last years without maintenance.

items.title: Pebbble
items.text: Every layer solves a specific constraint: The stone is the key.

items.title: Pebbble
items.text: The encryption key is derived from the NFC tag's unique serial number plus a timestamp, run through PBKDF2 with 100,000 iterations.

items.title: Pebbble
items.text: The key doesn't exist anywhere — not on a server, not in the app, not in the stone.

items.title: Pebbble
items.text: It is computed at the moment of reading from the physical object itself.

items.title: Pebbble
items.text: No accounts, no passwords. Physical possession is the only authentication.

items.title: Pebbble
items.text: IPFS distributes the voice. Content-addressed, decentralized.

items.title: Pebbble
items.text: Block one node, it routes through another. Block a domain — there is no domain to block.

items.title: Pebbble
items.text: A voice recorded in one country reaches a child in another regardless of what stands between them.

items.title: Pebbble
items.text: No central server. The storage provider never sees plaintext.

items.title: Pebbble
items.text: There is no database of messages, no server logs, no central point that can be compelled to reveal content.

items.title: Pebbble
items.text: The system is private by architecture, not by policy. There is no database of messages to subpoena.

items.title: Pebbble
items.text: If a parent's voice can reach an abducted child — safely, secretly, persistently — then the military family on deployment, the divorced couple across distance, the grandparent recording stories are all already served.

items.title: Pebbble
items.text: The app itself serves two fundamentally different experiences.

items.title: Pebbble
items.text: The reader must be poetic — the interface disappearing to offer nothing but the presence of a warm voice.

items.title: Pebbble
items.text: How do you design a screen that gets out of the way of a parent saying goodnight?

items.title: Pebbble
items.text: The writer is the opposite problem: recording, managing, reusing messages, adding music.

items.title: Pebbble
items.text: A parent recording a bedtime story at 11 PM after a long day cannot afford to fight an interface.

items.title: Pebbble
items.text: Simplicity is not a trend here — it is the constraint that guarantees the system gets used at all.

items.title: Pebbble
items.text: But the deeper split is not between reading and writing. It is between safety and evidence.

items.title: Pebbble
items.text: A child with their own phone keeps the voice always available.

items.title: Pebbble
items.text: Cached, ready whenever loneliness arrives at 2 AM. But what about a child using a borrowed device?

items.title: Pebbble
items.text: A shared tablet at a shelter? A phone belonging to someone who must not know what it accessed?

items.title: Pebbble
items.text: Ephemeral mode: the audio plays once. When the app closes, nothing remains.

items.title: Pebbble
items.text: No history, no cache, no evidence. The voice was heard, and then — nothing.

items.title: Pebbble
items.text: This is the hardest design constraint I've worked with. Not technically.

items.title: Pebbble
items.text: Emotionally. The idea that a child needs to hear their parent's voice in secret, and that evidence of hearing it could make things worse.

items.title: Pebbble
items.text: Accounts. An account is a target. It can be discovered, subpoenaed, locked.

items.title: Pebbble
items.text: The stone authenticates by physical possession. Nothing else.

items.title: Pebbble
items.text: Cloud storage. A server is a single point of failure and a single point of compulsion.

items.title: Pebbble
items.text: IPFS distributes content. No entity controls it.

items.title: Pebbble
items.text: Mobile app. An app in the app store can be found on the phone.

items.title: Pebbble
items.text: A PWA launched from an NFC tap operates ephemerally — no installation, no icon, no evidence.

items.title: Pebbble
items.text: The web is the delivery mechanism because the web can disappear.

items.title: Pebbble
items.text: User-created passwords. A child cannot remember a password. The stone itself is the password.

items.title: Pebbble
items.text: Pebbble is one of three projects using the same architecture: NFC tag on a physical object triggers a web experience with zero intermediary.

items.title: Pebbble
items.text: Drop — bottle cap triggers water map. Utility. Vrooom — wooden car triggers playground discovery.

items.title: Pebbble
items.text: Play. Pebbble — stone triggers encrypted voice. Presence.

items.title: Pebbble
items.text: Same pattern, different stakes. The NFC tap replaces the entire onboarding flow in all three.

items.title: Pebbble
items.text: But only Pebbble carries the weight of what happens when the physical object is the last connection between a parent and a child.

items.title: Pebbble
items.text: The architecture that makes Drop convenient makes Pebbble necessary.

items.title: Pebbble
items.text: IPFS permanence is the feature for the humanitarian case. Once pinned, the voice persists independent of any server, company, or jurisdiction.

items.title: Pebbble
items.text: But permanence has a cost. What about messages you later regret?

items.title: Pebbble
items.text: What about a child who grows up and wants the voice to stop?

items.title: Pebbble
items.text: This tension — between censorship resistance and the right to be forgotten — is unresolved.

items.title: Pebbble
items.text: I include this because most portfolios present resolved problems.

items.title: Pebbble
items.text: This one isn't resolved. That's honest.

items.title: Pebbble
items.text: As a child, it took me hours of practice to learn to skip stones across water.

items.title: Pebbble
items.text: But what I loved most about it — and certainly why I still love it — is not the throw.

items.title: Pebbble
items.text: It is what happens after. Each impact of the stone on the surface creates ripples that spread outward, connect to each other, and travel until they reach the shore.

items.title: Pebbble
items.text: Their final physical destination.

items.title: Pebbble
items.text: A voice recorded into a Pebbble does the same thing. It leaves one hand, crosses whatever distance stands between two people, and arrives — not as data, not as notification, but as presence.

items.title: Pebbble
items.text: A ripple that reaches the shore.

items.title: Pebbble
items.text: A stone. A voice. A child who remembers.

items.title: Senz
items.text: Making sense of ideas — turning a sketch into a deployed prototype without a developer in the loop.

items.title: Senz
items.text: Why: Large organisations lose most of their internal ideas to a validation cycle too expensive to run.

items.title: Senz
items.text: Four disciplines, months of sprint, a six-figure budget — most experts never get permission to test what they already know.

items.title: Senz
items.text: What: A platform that lets non-designers and non-developers sketch an interface on paper, have it read by a sovereign vision model, and deploy as production code in the company's own design system — without a developer in the loop.

items.title: Senz
items.text: Outcome: Employees inside Allianz tested radical business ideas in days instead of quarters, including one that opened a new insurance market segment through a service the standard product pipeline would never have produced.

items.title: Senz
items.text: Senz was a prototyping tool built at Kaiser X Labs and deployed inside Allianz.

items.title: Senz
items.text: It gave domain experts — claims handlers, underwriters, product managers — direct authorship over working product prototypes, without a developer in the chain.

items.title: Senz
items.text: I led the project with Sven Martinov and Olivier Gonthier as the core team, inside Kaiser X Labs, Allianz's innovation studio.

items.title: Senz
items.text: Shipped seven years before Figma Make.

items.title: Senz
items.text: Large organisations spent the last decade on digital transformation, secretly hoping it would keep startups and market disruptors away from their business.

items.title: Senz
items.text: Each new framework, method, and tool they stacked on was meant to make them faster.

items.title: Senz
items.text: Instead, it raised the locking bar on budget approval — committing a full team of designers, researchers, and developers to build an MVP that was already outdated before launch.

items.title: Senz
items.text: They didn't need more matter. They needed to rearrange what they had.

items.title: Senz
items.text: Organisations are closed systems of a different kind of matter.

items.title: Senz
items.text: Frameworks, components, design systems, data, business logic, flows, APIs, and the people who understand them — the latent potentials sitting inside every large company.

items.title: Senz
items.text: None of it is missing. Most is underused, mis-combined, or defended by whichever team currently owns its shape.

items.title: Senz
items.text: Lavoisier, working on combustion in the 1780s, established a principle that dismantled alchemy: in a closed system, nothing new is created and nothing is lost.

items.title: Senz
items.text: Everything is transformed.

items.title: Senz
items.text: Senz was built on this principle. Momentum had come first — a tool we built to let non-experts contribute to Allianz's Angular atomic library.

items.title: Senz
items.text: It failed. The learning curve was too steep, and the people it was supposed to empower could not climb it quickly enough to stay engaged.

items.title: Senz
items.text: The system was sophisticated. That was the problem.

items.title: Senz
items.text: A few months later, in a meeting about the coming design system, a home claims expert walked to the whiteboard and started sketching a First Notification of Loss — boxes, hero, the few inputs a customer needs to report that something has gone wrong.

items.title: Senz
items.text: She asked the builders whether their components could handle the cases and logic she was drawing.

items.title: Senz
items.text: My mind slipped sideways, to Google Photos — how it had quietly crossed the threshold where labelling an image was the same thing as reading it.

items.title: Senz
items.text: Pixels into signal. Signal into structured matter the system could act on.

items.title: Senz
items.text: Paper and pen. The most radical and simple input on earth. The medium people reach for long before they turn to a computer, available in every office and every country, affordable at every economic tier.

items.title: Senz
items.text: If Google could turn photos into structured matter at scale, we could turn drawings into production components the same way.

items.title: Senz
items.text: Momentum had tried to teach experts a new tool. Senz would meet them at the tool they already used.

items.title: Senz
items.text: Senz was built on three principles, held together. Affordance.

items.title: Senz
items.text: The interface mirrored the simplicity of the raw material it accepted.

items.title: Senz
items.text: A canvas, a side toolbar, a predict button. No dashboard, no project setup.

items.title: Senz
items.text: Input arrived through whichever surface the user already had — a phone photo via the companion app, direct drawing on a touch-enabled laptop, drag-and-drop of pre-made wireframe elements, SVG or image upload.

items.title: Senz
items.text: Data arrived the same way: spreadsheet, CSV, database endpoint, one click through connectors.

items.title: Senz
items.text: Senz never contained data. It managed the flow between systems that already held it.

items.title: Senz
items.text: Assistance. The model was a translation layer, never a generative one.

items.title: Senz
items.text: The system recognised the user's intent but did not produce it.

items.title: Senz
items.text: Completed steps folded and dismissed as progress was made, clearing the canvas without erasing the path.

items.title: Senz
items.text: Real-time collaboration ran through mandate roles — admin, designer, reviewer, approver — so different experts could author different layers of the same prototype without colliding.

items.title: Senz
items.text: Transparency. The model was trained by design never to pretend.

items.title: Senz
items.text: Confidence thresholds were tuned to surface uncertainty rather than hide it — if the system did not recognise a shape, it said so.

items.title: Senz
items.text: Every decision was the user's, and therefore auditable by the user.

items.title: Senz
items.text: The stack was there to serve, not to harvest.

items.title: Senz
items.text: The companion app preprocessing pipeline. Users couldn't be asked to stage their shot.

items.title: Senz
items.text: A phone photo of a real whiteboard, with glare, angle, and other people's notes in the background, had to be readable by the production system — no special paper, no careful framing, no instructions.

items.title: Senz
items.text: Browser-based capture wasn't technically possible at the time, so the companion app handled its own computer-vision preprocessing before the main model ever saw the image: object extraction, foreign-item removal, drop-shadow and flare filtering, perspective correction.

items.title: Senz
items.text: Affordance enforced upstream, not just in the UI.

items.title: Senz
items.text: One predict button, not continuous recognition. The model ran on our own on-prem hardware.

items.title: Senz
items.text: Continuous prediction would have burned compute for marginal UX gain, and we refused it on ecological grounds.

items.title: Senz
items.text: The consequence reshaped the interaction: a deliberate predict action invited the user to think first, draw, and then translate.

items.title: Senz
items.text: The pause before pressing predict was a thinking space the tool preserved on purpose.

items.title: Senz
items.text: A two-stage recognition pipeline. A wireframe is not a grid of pixels.

items.title: Senz
items.text: It's a document with layout structure — a button is a button partly because of where it sits in the composition, not only because of how it looks.

items.title: Senz
items.text: The recognition ran in two stages to honour that: a detection model (RetinaNet) located the shapes on the page, and a classification model (LayoutLM) read each region in its spatial context, deciding what the shape was given what surrounded it.

items.title: Senz
items.text: The system understood composition, not just shapes.

items.title: Senz
items.text: Direct manipulation on the canvas, versioning for tested journeys.

items.title: Senz
items.text: The drawing was live material. Marks could be erased, redrawn, moved, scaled at any point — the canvas worked the way a sketchbook works, and adjustments happened in the drawing itself.

items.title: Senz
items.text: Versioning operated at a different layer. Once a prototype had been predicted and deployed — run against users, shown to stakeholders, tested in the wild — that version was preserved.

items.title: Senz
items.text: The user could then branch the project, redraw the canvas, and produce a new version to compare against the first.

items.title: Senz
items.text: A/B testing was an intentional capability, not a side effect: projects could be cloned, deployed online with public or password-gated access, and evaluated side by side against real users.

items.title: Senz
items.text: Side-by-side prediction, then toggle. The first release showed the original drawing and the recognised version side by side by default.

items.title: Senz
items.text: In testing we watched users begin to contort their sketches to help the model read them — the draw-predict-infinity-loop — and we moved side-by-side to a toggle.

items.title: Senz
items.text: Transparency, on demand. Default-visible uncertainty had become its own attention tax.

items.title: Senz
items.text: On-device, sovereign model. No remote API calls. No third-party cloud dependency that could change its terms or lose compliance posture mid-project.

items.title: Senz
items.text: This was a 2018 decision that most 2026 AI products still have not made.

items.title: Senz
items.text: The outcome was not a metric. It was a capacity. Senz bypassed the six-figure budget gate that had stood in front of every internal test.

items.title: Senz
items.text: No one needed approval to test a business idea. A claims handler, an underwriter, a product manager could now assemble a working prototype from a sketch in days rather than quarters, deploy it, run it against real data, and archive it when it didn't work — without a developer in the chain, without a design sprint, without a proposal deck.

items.title: Senz
items.text: The unit of measurement shifted from the idea to the test. Failure became cheaper than the meeting held to debate it.

items.title: Senz
items.text: One specific test proves the capacity worked. An in-house agent working on bike insurance — a single employee, not a consultant — used Senz to test an idea the company would not have generated otherwise.

items.title: Senz
items.text: The observation was plain: many urban cyclists were not ready to commit to monthly or yearly premiums, and the institutional default was to write them off.

items.title: Senz
items.text: The hypothesis was that this was the wrong gesture.

items.title: Senz
items.text: What if, instead of turning these people away, the company offered them a near-zero-cost service — something small, useful, oriented toward preventing the risk they were not yet ready to insure against?

items.title: Senz
items.text: Not a discount. Not a trial. A caring gesture: the business acknowledging it was about risk reduction, not only premium collection.

items.title: Senz
items.text: Senz made it testable in days. The prototype was assembled from existing customer data, infrastructure, and risk models — recombined into a service that would never have survived the budget approval required to build it conventionally.

items.title: Senz
items.text: The segment the company had previously been unable to reach began to engage — not with the product, but with the posture behind it.

items.title: Senz
items.text: Trust was the outcome. The service was only its instrument.

items.title: Senz
items.text: Technology like this will revolutionize the way we innovate and supports non-designers and non-developers on their way to build a digital product by themselves.

items.title: Senz
items.text: — Kai Kölsch, Founder & CEO, Seedbox Ventures

items.title: Senz
items.text: The matter is already there. The work doesn't belong where it used to.

items.title: Senz
items.text: It stops being the specialist's — the consultant, the lab, the people with permission to conjure.

items.title: Senz
items.text: It belongs to anyone who touches the matter. The CTO whose systems already contain latent capability.

items.title: Senz
items.text: The designer who has seen what the customers actually need. The claims expert at the whiteboard.

items.title: Senz
items.text: These are the people who already know. Most of the time, they are waiting for permission.

items.title: Senz
items.text: Senz was one instrument for granting that permission. There will be others.

items.title: Senz
items.text: The matter is rarely the obstacle. I led the project end-to-end at Kaiser X Labs (Allianz): product concept and design, full UX, end-to-end training dataset and labeling strategy, multi-framework reasoning, and the research-insights connectors that let us validate business models on real data.

items.title: Senz
items.text: The core team was three. Sven Martinov : Built the four ML models.

items.title: Senz
items.text: Deployed, ran, and scaled the on-prem inference servers. Scaled the labeling studio.

items.title: Senz
items.text: Owned the FastAPI connectors across the ML and no-code surfaces.

items.title: Senz
items.text: Olivier Gonthier : Rebuilt the multimodal interface — touch, pen, drag-and-drop, upload.

items.title: Senz
items.text: Built the multi-framework code-mapping engine and the conditional business-logic builder.

items.title: Senz
items.text: Two earlier contributors shaped Senz before the core team came together.

items.title: Senz
items.text: Jakob Berhend : Design and documentation in Senz's early stage.

items.title: Senz
items.text: Kept the project's progress legible as the concept took shape.

items.title: Senz
items.text: Maksim Kipot : Built the front-end of the original Senz prototype.

items.title: Senz
items.text: Björn Frank sponsored the deployment with continuous support and a visionary commitment to scale the product in-house.

items.title: Senz
items.text: Flutter companion app with custom computer-vision preprocessing · RetinaNet for region detection, LayoutLM for contextual classification · on-prem inference, no remote API calls · multi-framework output (Angular, Vue, React) targeting numerous design systems including Allianz's internal library, IBM Carbon, Google Material, Microsoft Fluent · webhook and connector-based integrations · declarative flow and logic composition layer · versioned prototypes with public or password-gated deployment.

items.title: Vrooom
items.text: What: A wooden toy with an NFC chip links to a playground discovery PWA.

items.title: Vrooom
items.text: Children check in, earn badges, print them through the company website, color them, glue them into a handmade passport.

items.title: Vrooom
items.text: Every print sends a parent to the product catalog — without an ad, a popup, or a captured email.

items.title: Vrooom
items.text: Why: Children's apps monetize attention. Growth hacking monetizes trust.

items.title: Vrooom
items.text: Both extract more than they give. Vrooom inverts the model: the utility earns the visit, the visit earns the discovery, the discovery earns the next purchase — if the product deserves it.

items.title: Vrooom
items.text: How: NFC as entry point, zero accounts, zero tracking, E2E encrypted WebRTC bridge to website for printing.

items.title: Vrooom
items.text: The product serves an immediate need with no compromise. The business grows because people come back, not because they're brought back.

items.title: Vrooom
items.text: Proof: 15 seconds of screen time per session. Zero data sent to any server.

items.title: Vrooom
items.text: The growth channel is a parent choosing to print something for their child.

items.title: Vrooom
items.text: -- Role: Systems Designer & Product Strategist Key supporter: Thomas Duester — kept pushing when I was ready to move on.

items.title: Vrooom
items.text: Some projects survive because someone else refuses to let them die.

items.title: Vrooom
items.text: Stack: Vanilla JS, Three. js, Leaflet, Overpass API, Valhalla routing, Dexie.

items.title: Vrooom
items.text: js Design metric: Screen time measured in seconds per interaction, not minutes.

items.title: Vrooom
items.text: A child runs to the bench where her father sits. She holds up a stick — a wand, perhaps, or a sword, or something that has no name yet because she is still deciding.

items.title: Vrooom
items.text: She wants him to see.

items.title: Vrooom
items.text: He glances up from his phone. "That's nice, honey. " His eyes return to the screen.

items.title: Vrooom
items.text: She waits. The stick lowers. She walks back to the grass, alone.

items.title: Vrooom
items.text: The phone is not the villain. The phone is the symptom. The villain is the exhaustion, the isolation, the impossible demands placed on parents who have no village.

items.title: Vrooom
items.text: The phone fills the vacuum we created.

items.title: Vrooom
items.text: But what else could fill it? Children's apps are a billion-dollar industry built on a single transaction: silence purchased with screen time.

items.title: Vrooom
items.text: Engagement is the metric. Retention is the goal. The app succeeds when the child does not look up.

items.title: Vrooom
items.text: Behind this industry sits another one: growth hacking. Captured emails.

items.title: Vrooom
items.text: Retargeting pixels. Push notifications. Streak mechanics. Dark patterns dressed as engagement.

items.title: Vrooom
items.text: The business model requires the user to be brought back — because the product alone is not worth returning to.

items.title: Vrooom
items.text: What if the product was worth returning to? A wooden car. Beech — closed grain, food-safe, built to outlast the child who holds it.

items.title: Vrooom
items.text: Inside: an NFC tag. Tap it to a parent's phone and a PWA opens — a playground discovery app that checks in at parks, earns badges, and gets out of the way.

items.title: Vrooom
items.text: Fifteen seconds of screen time per session. No account. No data sent anywhere.

items.title: Vrooom
items.text: No push notifications. No streaks.

items.title: Vrooom
items.text: The app serves one need: a child wants to explore. It serves it completely, then disappears.

items.title: Vrooom
items.text: Brands win more from being remembered for what they leave behind than from what they took.

items.title: Vrooom
items.text: The toy does not need the phone. The phone needs the parent.

items.title: Vrooom
items.text: This is the foundation. A product that respects its user has earned something no retargeting pixel can buy: trust.

items.title: Vrooom
items.text: A parent who trusts the product comes back. Not because they were reminded.

items.title: Vrooom
items.text: Because they chose to.

items.title: Vrooom
items.text: The shape descends from a childhood memory — matchbox cars with cork wheels.

items.title: Vrooom
items.text: Why those toys lasted was not their complexity. It was their simplicity.

items.title: Vrooom
items.text: They were substrates for play, not scripts for it. No doors, no windows, no driver.

items.title: Vrooom
items.text: Every detail removed is a story the child gets to add.

items.title: Vrooom
items.text: Hand-planed from rectangular blocks — finding the right taper, grip, and weight happened physically, not in CAD.

items.title: Vrooom
items.text: The bottom tapers at front and back — not decoration, but function.

items.title: Vrooom
items.text: Push it like a friction toy and the taper lifts it slightly, prevents scratching, makes the glide smooth.

items.title: Vrooom
items.text: There is a Japanese carpentry principle: build it in a way that it lasts as long as it took the tree to grow.

items.title: Vrooom
items.text: The first prototypes went to neighborhood kids. No instructions, no explanation.

items.title: Vrooom
items.text: They connected with the object before anyone mentioned the app.

items.title: Vrooom
items.text: The wood, the weight, the shape. If the physical object does not stand alone — if it needs the digital to justify itself — the design has failed.

items.title: Vrooom
items.text: The NFC inside is an expansion, not a requirement.

items.title: Vrooom
items.text: The design goal for the first moment a child taps the car to a parent's phone: nothing less than magic.

items.title: Vrooom
items.text: Eyes shining. The thing in their hand was hiding this all along.

items.title: Vrooom
items.text: A product people love is a product people return to. That is not a marketing insight.

items.title: Vrooom
items.text: It is a design decision. No avatar, no account, no login. The child's identity in the app is their wooden car.

items.title: Vrooom
items.text: The NFC tag carries a URL pointing to a car configuration — a 3D model with mapped parts, colors, and sounds.

items.title: Vrooom
items.text: Tap the car to the phone, and it appears on screen: a rendered wooden toy that spins, responds to touch, and revs its engine.

items.title: Vrooom
items.text: The 3D viewer captures a side-view snapshot that becomes the child's marker on the map.

items.title: Vrooom
items.text: Their car drives across the neighborhood as they walk.

items.title: Vrooom
items.text: No "select a playground" step. No trip planning. The child walks.

items.title: Vrooom
items.text: When they arrive — a playground, a park, a pool — they tap "I'm here.

items.title: Vrooom
items.text: " Fresh GPS, nearest match within 150 metres, visit logged.

items.title: Vrooom
items.text: The badge system is designed to end in paper, not pixels. Playground badges — one per unique place visited Regular badges — earned after 10 visits to the same place Milestone badges — shields for 1, 5, 10, 25, 50 unique playgrounds

items.title: Vrooom
items.text: All badges are SVG line art. Intentionally uncolored. The badge page connects to the Vrooom website via end-to-end encrypted WebRTC — a single button, no account, no cloud.

items.title: Vrooom
items.text: The 3D car viewer doubles as a coloring-book generator — choose an angle and it renders a line-art outline ready for printing.

items.title: Vrooom
items.text: Print the badges. Cut along the lines. Color them in. Color the car.

items.title: Vrooom
items.text: Glue them into a handmade passport. The badges end in paper.

items.title: Vrooom
items.text: But the path to paper passes through the Vrooom website. That visit is not accidental.

items.title: Vrooom
items.text: A parent standing at a printer, waiting for badge sheets, is standing inside the company's product catalog.

items.title: Vrooom
items.text: No banner. No popup. No "you might also like. " They came because the app was useful.

items.title: Vrooom
items.text: They stay because the products are visible. They return because their child earned new badges.

items.title: Vrooom
items.text: This is led-growth without the growth hacking. No captured email.

items.title: Vrooom
items.text: No retargeting pixel. No notification asking them to come back.

items.title: Vrooom
items.text: The utility earns the visit. The visit earns the discovery. The discovery earns the next purchase — if the product deserves it.

items.title: Vrooom
items.text: Every children's app monetizes attention. Vrooom monetizes the moment a parent chooses to print something for their child.

items.title: Vrooom
items.text: The difference is who holds the power in that transaction.

items.title: Vrooom
items.text: Gamification. No points, no streaks, no leaderboards. The moment you add streaks, you add anxiety.

items.title: Vrooom
items.text: A playground is not a competition.

items.title: Vrooom
items.text: Social features. No friends, no sharing, no "see where other kids are.

items.title: Vrooom
items.text: " Social features shift focus from exploration to performance.

items.title: Vrooom
items.text: The child should discover playgrounds because they are curious, not because their friend did.

items.title: Vrooom
items.text: Turn-by-turn navigation. Vrooom shows walking routes when asked, but does not guide.

items.title: Vrooom
items.text: A child walking to a playground should look at the world, not at a screen.

items.title: Vrooom
items.text: Photo capture. Rejected — it puts the phone back in the child's hands at the moment they should be playing.

items.title: Vrooom
items.text: The check-in is the record. The badge is the memory.

items.title: Vrooom
items.text: Child-held device. The phone belongs to the parent. If the child holds the phone, the phone becomes the toy.

items.title: Vrooom
items.text: If the parent holds the phone, the phone becomes the bridge.

items.title: Vrooom
items.text: Ads, emails, push notifications. The conventional growth toolkit.

items.title: Vrooom
items.text: Every one of them trades user trust for a short-term metric.

items.title: Vrooom
items.text: The product grows by being worth returning to, or it does not grow.

items.title: Vrooom
items.text: A shape that carries no date cannot become dated. A material that ages cannot become obsolete.

items.title: Vrooom
items.text: Fifty years from now, the same car will feel the same in a child's hand, will invite the same open stories, will wait for the same imagination to bring it alive.

items.title: Vrooom
items.text: And perhaps, by then, it will carry something more. The passport stamps from trips that became legends.

items.title: Vrooom
items.text: The layers of memory pressed into an object, invisible as the NFC chip, present as the wood's weight.

items.title: Vrooom
items.text: The toy is not the legacy. The play is the legacy. The toy is just what holds it.

items.title: Vrooom
items.text: Vrooom is the third project in the physical-digital-bridge cluster: Drop — bottle cap triggers water map.

items.title: Vrooom
items.text: Utility. Pebbble — stone triggers encrypted voice. Presence.

items.title: Vrooom
items.text: Vrooom — wooden car triggers playground discovery. Play.

items.title: Vrooom
items.text: But Vrooom adds something the others don't: the output is physical too.

items.title: Vrooom
items.text: The digital layer is sandwiched between two physical ones — a wooden car on one end, a paper passport on the other.

items.title: Vrooom
items.text: And Vrooom carries a question the others don't ask. Drop proves that public infrastructure can replace proprietary APIs.

items.title: Vrooom
items.text: Pebbble proves that privacy can be enforced by architecture.

items.title: Vrooom
items.text: Vrooom demonstrates something else: a working system where the business model and the user's interest are structurally aligned — not by policy, not by promise, but by architecture.

items.title: Vrooom
items.text: The parent goes to the website because they want to, not because they were nudged.

items.title: Vrooom
items.text: The companies that need this thinking are the ones starting to realize that the extraction model has a ceiling.

items.title: Vrooom
items.text: Users leave. Regulation tightens. Brand trust erodes. The ones who figure out how to grow by giving more than they take will outlast the ones still optimizing click-through rates.

items.title: Vrooom
items.text: A car in the hand. A playground around the corner. The phone already forgotten.
